papers.title: Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification
papers.abstract: Medical image classifiers require not only high accuracy but also reliable predictions under small input perturbations. Certified robustness provides mathematical guarantees of prediction stability, but preserving these guarantees when adapting pretrained models to new tasks remains challenging. We propose a fine-tuning approach based on quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly layers that preserves the Lipschitz bounds of pretrained certified networks. Inspired by quantum circuits of reconfigurable beam splitters, these layers preserve orthogonality by construction using only $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ trainable parameters. Their structured design enables efficient classical implementation and offers a path toward future quantum implementations with logarithmic circuit depth under suitable connectivity assumptions. Controlled experiments on MNIST and MedMNIST demonstrate improved certified robustness compared with conventional alternatives and, in the DermaMNIST transfer, greater resistance to the tested attacks than low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then apply it to trichoscopic image classification for alopecia diagnosis and alopecia areata activity assessment. By adapting a certified ImageNet-pretrained network, butterfly fine-tuning achieves approximately twice the certified accuracy of conventional fine-tuning and LoRA, with comparable classification accuracy on the same backbone and data split and similar empirical resistance to the tested adversarial attacks. Larger robustness guarantees, including certificates covering certain image-processing transformations, can be obtained at the cost of reduced accuracy. These results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired butterfly layers for parameter-efficient adaptation of medical image classifiers while preserving the mathematical guarantees underlying certified robustness.

papers.title: Postselection on Halting and Reductions to the Halting Problem
papers.abstract: A probabilistic Turing machine is an ordinary Turing machine that may also toss fair coins, with no limit on its running time or memory. If it always halts, it decides only computable problems. Aaronson et al. studied machines that may run forever on some coin tosses, with the answer read only from the runs that halt. Suppose the correct answer must be more than twice as likely as the wrong one. They showed that these machines decide exactly the problems solvable with a fixed list of questions about the halting problem. They asked what happens when the correct answer need only be the more likely one. We show that the machines then decide exactly the problems solvable by asking such questions one after another, each chosen after the earlier answers. We also show that the factor two can be replaced by any fixed factor greater than one. A machine may promise two numbers: a lower bound on its probability of halting, and a lower bound on its probability of being right when it halts. From these two numbers we compute exactly how many questions fixed in advance the machine can replace. The main idea is that probability acts as a budget for how often a computable guess may change its mind. The results extend to oracle machines and to machines nested inside each other. Quantum machines decide the same problems.

papers.title: Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Eavesdropping in BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
papers.abstract: BB84 quantum key distribution derives its security from a physical guarantee that any eavesdropper disturbs the channel in a statistically detectable way. Prior work evaluates this by assuming Eve attacks at a fixed, analytically optimized rate. We examine what happens when Eve is modeled instead as a learning agent. Classical reinforcement learning is used, specifically tabular Q-Learning, SARSA, and Double Q-Learning, to adaptive BB84 eavesdropping. This formulates the attacker's decision as a Markov Decision Process where the agent observes Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) feedback and decides, qubit by qubit, whether to intercept or pass. Experiments span three channel noise levels ($\mu_{ch}\in\{1\%,3\%,5\%\}$) and are validated across five independent random seeds (45 training runs per condition, 10,000 episodes each). Against the best non-adaptive analytical baseline, Q-Learning reduces detection from $99.4\%$ to $0.28\%\pm0.27\%$ at $\mu_{ch}=1\%$ while extracting approximately 10.5 correct bits per episode. This is a 355-fold reduction that is statistically significant ($p=0.020$, Mann-Whitney $U$ test). We also report the spontaneous emergence of an end-game burst, where agents independently learn to surge their attack rate at the final block. This exploit vanishes under randomized checkpoint intervals while stealth performance remains statistically indistinguishable. These results motivate the inclusion of adaptive adversary baselines in quantum cryptographic security evaluations.

papers.title: No Convergence in Learned Eavesdropping-Detection Dynamics for BB84 Quantum Key Distribution
papers.abstract: In prior work we showed that a reinforcement-learning eavesdropper can intercept BB84 quantum key distribution while holding the quantum bit error rate below the abort threshold and keeping a usable distillable key. In this paper we ask whether an equally adaptive learning detector can close this stealth window. We cast the interaction as an alternating best-response game between a tabular eavesdropper and a tabular threshold-adapting detector. We measure exploitability, which is the detection rate and distillable key fraction achieved by a fresh attacker best-responding to the final detector. Across three learning rules (Q-Learning, SARSA, Double Q-Learning), three channel-noise levels, and a uniform false-alarm discipline, the dynamics do not settle out to twenty rounds. The exploitability does not approach a fixed point, and its round-to-round swings do not decay. Two controls, one retraining the attacker against a frozen defender and one retraining the defender against a frozen attacker, show that the swings on each side match the variance of the best-response procedure itself. The dynamics fluctuate at the scale of best-response variance rather than converging, with neither player settling to a fixed response. The behavior is noise-dependent, and the stealth window stays open at the low noise where practical QKD operates. The defender contains the attacker on average at intermediate noise without the contest settling, and at high noise the channel rather than the learned policy suppresses the attack. As a candidate mechanism we examine a last-mover information asymmetry, supported by significant anti-persistence at intermediate noise and consistent with best-response noise at low noise. The results suggest that a learned detector cannot be certified from any single round, and that closing the window calls for breaking the information structure rather than out-adapting the attacker.

papers.title: A Quasipolynomial Quantum Algorithm for the Vector Dihedral Coset Problem with Smooth Modulus
papers.abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for the vector dihedral coset problem over $\mathbb{Z}_q^n$, in which the goal is to recover $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n$ given independent samples of the form $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|{0,\mathbf{x}}\rangle+|{1,\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{s}}\rangle\bigr)$, for $\mathbf{x}\sim \mathbb{Z}_q^n$. When the modulus $q$ is $B$-smooth, the algorithm uses $n^{O(B^{1+o(1)}\log q)}B^{O(B^{2+o(1)}\log q)}$ samples and time. For $B = \mathrm{polylog}(n)$ and $q=\mathrm{poly}(n)$, this gives a quasipolynomial time- and sample-complexity. This extends the previously known quasipolynomial-time result for power-of-two moduli (Bonnetain, Naya-Plasencia, ASIACRYPT 2018; Bai, Jangir, Kirshanova, Ngo, Youmans, CRYPTO 2025). The algorithm proceeds by reducing the modulus one prime factor $p | q$ at a time. The key ingredient is a sieving procedure that clears the non-linear terms in the phase modulo $p$ via an algorithm of Ivanyos, Santha (TCS 2017) that finds non-zero $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{F}_p^\ell$ such that $\sum_{i \in [\ell]} u_i^d \mathbf{a}_i = 0 \mod p$ for degrees $1 \le d \le p-1$, given vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_\ell \in \mathbb{F}_p^n$ as input. The algorithm also applies to the extrapolated dihedral coset problem (EDCP) introduced by Brakerski, Kirshanova, Stehl\'e, Wen (PKC 2018), which is known to be equivalent to LWE in the polynomial sample regime. However, our result does not yield a new attack on LWE in any regime, precisely because the known reduction from LWE to EDCP provides only polynomially many clean samples, whereas our algorithm requires quasipolynomially many samples. The main algorithm was obtained in a GPT-5.6 Sol conversation prompted by the author; the author is responsible for all statements, proofs, and correctness. Concurrent work of Boucher, Fouque, Shen gives an algorithm with similar guarantees for prime-power moduli.

papers.title: Separations Between Randomized and Exact Quantum Query Complexity for Boolean Functions
papers.abstract: We construct a family of total Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{tot}}$ whose randomized and exact quantum query complexities satisfy $R(F_{\mathrm{tot}}) \ge Q_E(F_{\mathrm{tot}})^{2-o(1)}$. Chiruvella, Kayal, Mittal, Paraashar, and Saurabh (2026) also obtained a nearly quadratic separation for total functions in the query model by a different method. For every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we construct a family of partial Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{par}}$ on $n$ bits satisfying $Q_E(F_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(1)$ and $R(F_{\mathrm{par}})=\Omega_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$. This matches the asymptotic separation previously obtained with bounded error (STOC 2021; SICOMP 2023). Lifting yields a family of partial communication functions $G_{\mathrm{par}}$ with $Q_E^{\mathrm{cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ and $R^{\mathrm{pub,cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=\Omega_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $n$ is the total number of input bits held by the two parties.

papers.title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
papers.abstract: Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

papers.title: On the effects of emulated quantum layers on CNN performance and explainability for OCT and dementia imaging
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical convolutional neural networks have been proposed as an alternative to classical deep learning models. However, executing network components on quantum hardware imposes fundamental limitations, such as gradient estimation through repeated measurements, and increasing the number of qubits can lead to trainability problems such as barren plateaus. Moreover, the reported success of these hybrid networks has been linked to quantum architectures that can be efficiently simulated on classical computers. We investigate whether small, classically simulated quantum circuits can serve as useful components within larger models, as a substitute for purely classical layers. We present a systematic comparison between a Hybrid Quantum-inspired CNN (HQiCNN) and standard CNN architectures, where the models differ only in a single intermediate layer: an emulated quantum circuit in the HQiCNN and classical counterparts in the CNN. The models are evaluated on two medical imaging datasets while varying training set size, learning rate, batch size, circuit entanglement and observable se. Under a strict parameter budget, the HQiCNN outperforms the classical baselines. When the classical layer is given more parameters, overall performance becomes comparable, with the HQiCNN showing improvements only in the intermediate-data regime. Removing entanglement yields comparable performance and richer observable sets yield no performance improvement. Finally, we introduce two SHAP-based metrics for comparing model explanations, $|$SHAP$|$IoU and EMD$_{\mathrm{pos}}$. They show that all architectures attend to anatomically plausible regions, and that the spatial attention agreement between them increases with training set size. These results indicate that, under specific data regimes, quantum-inspired hybrid models are a competitive alternative to classical CNNs for medical image classification.

papers.title: QuSema: Detecting Silent Bugs in Quantum Libraries via Quantum-knowledge-enhanced Agents
papers.abstract: Quantum libraries are now critical infrastructure for quantum algorithm development, yet their correctness remains difficult to test. Existing testing techniques mainly rely on failure-based or comparison-based oracles, exposing bugs only when executions fail, violate runtime checks, or disagree with another implementation. Their applicability is limited when suitable execution-based oracles are unavailable, leaving some silent bugs undetected. Such missed bugs can produce incorrect results that propagate into experimental conclusions, simulation studies, and algorithmic designs. Here we present QuSema, an autonomous testing agent for finding silent bugs in quantum libraries. QuSema uses constraints from quantum semantics and documentation as a source-level semantic oracle to assess whether implementation logic can produce invalid outputs from valid inputs. It operates through an agentic loop that repeatedly inspects library API documentation and source code, reasons about the intended behavior of quantum operations, identifies potential semantic deviations, and validates them by generating executable tests through library APIs. Guided by quantum-domain reasoning, QuSema turns high-level behavioral mismatches into concrete, user-triggerable bug reports, enabling it to uncover non-crash defects. We implement QuSema for Qiskit and PennyLane. On a benchmark of 20 historical silent bugs, QuSema achieves higher mean bug relocation counts than Claude Code and Codex, with the DeepSeek configuration costing less than Claude Code. QuSema also discovers 40 previously unknown bugs confirmed by the developers, including 30 silent bugs.

papers.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. Its local message passing keeps computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. We further embed GraphMP in a beam-search algorithm that progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. To turn this decoding effort into lasting improvements, we propose the decoder model factory, a paradigm for training successive models on data collected by earlier models during decoding. In our implementation, verified search trajectories provide reusable training data for distilling knowledge into subsequent models. Across generations, the model factory yields a search-enhanced decoder that is broadly competitive with Relay-BP. On the largest code block, which encodes $4612$ logical qubits, it achieves a lower logical error rate and about $20$ times the decoding throughput of the standard Relay-BP baseline. These results motivate a coupled quantum-classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning adapts the models to changing noise conditions. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that continually produces high-performance, low-latency decoders for evolving quantum hardware.

papers.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
papers.abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.57x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 12x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

papers.title: Application-Oriented Evaluation of CPU/GPU Quantum Simulators: From Foundational Circuits to Quantum Chemistry
papers.abstract: Quantum computing simulators underpin the development and prototyping of quantum algorithms, yet the practical choice between competing software stacks and their CPU and GPU backends is rarely guided by application-oriented evidence. We present a systematic, quantum hardware-agnostic evaluation of two widely used stacks, CUDA-Q and Qiskit, selected as the simulators closest to production execution paths, across CPU and GPU backends, and across single- and double-precision arithmetic. The evaluation spans foundational utility circuits (GHZ-state preparation and QFT/QFT$^\dagger$ mirror circuits) through applied quantum chemistry (Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) energy estimation with standard UCCSD and a depth-reduced LCNot-UCCSD ansatz, and direct sampling on hydrogen chains up to 32 qubits). The results yield concrete selection guidance: GPU-accelerated double precision delivers consistent speedups, typically $2\times$ to $10\times$ for tractable application workloads and substantially larger at the widest circuits up to $100\times$ or more, and governs the maximum simulable system size under fixed compute memory, while CPU statevector backends and Qiskit Aer remain competitive, and at times preferable, at low qubit counts and wide but shallow circuits. We demonstrate the practical payoff of this guidance by extending an in-house developed QSCI(LCNot-UCCSD)-RBM electronic-structure workflow, previously constrained to a 16-qubit active space on a CPU, to a 32-qubit (10 electrons, 16 orbitals) active space with GPU acceleration, completing a 20-point potential-energy-surface scan of N$_{2}$ in the cc-pVDZ basis. This end-to-end evaluation establishes that the principled simulator selection translates directly into expanded scientific reach and faster algorithmic prototyping.

papers.title: $Q$-Drive: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Control Framework for Nonlinear Vehicular Dynamics
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce $Q$-Drive, a hybrid quantum-classical control framework for nonlinear vehicular dynamics that integrates variational quantum circuits (VQCs) with classical optimization, encoding vehicle states into a quantum Hilbert space via angle embedding, applying a trainable quantum ansatz to generate control signals, and refining circuit parameters through gradient descent to minimize tracking error and control effort. The proposed $Q$-Drive is evaluated in two settings: Single-vehicle control of nonlinear bicycle dynamics and a decoupled multi-vehicle swarm scenario with fleet sizes ranging from $N=2$ to $N=50$, demonstrating that the approach achieves exceptionally low control effort, reduced by orders of magnitude compared to classical model predictive control (MPC) and linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) benchmarks in the single-vehicle case, with average per-vehicle control effort decreasing by over 60\% from $N=2$ to $N=50$ in the swarm setting. Beyond empirical evaluation, we establish rigorous stability guarantees by constructing a composite Lyapunov function that jointly captures classical tracking dynamics and quantum-state purity. This analysis proves that the closed-loop system remains ultimately uniformly bounded under arbitrary road conditions, including inclined, rough, and curvilinear surfaces, as well as in the presence of quantum decoherence on the NISQ hardware, with explicit critical thresholds linking decoherence rates to environmental adversity. For the swarm extension, a theoretical bound is derived that shows that the average per-vehicle control effort decreases inversely with fleet size, in agreement with empirical observations. $Q$-Drive offers a promising direction for intelligent transportation systems by enabling robust, energy-efficient, and scalable vehicle control under complex real-world driving conditions.

papers.title: Shallow Clifford circuits on square lattices
papers.abstract: We study the depth of CZ circuits, Clifford state preparation, and Clifford unitary synthesis over the two-dimensional square lattice. A programmable circuit on a $2{\times}k$ ladder ($n{=}2k$) implements an arbitrary CZ computation in depth at most $\frac{3n}{2}{+}3$ up to reversal of both rails. This improves the best-known LNN (Linear Nearest-Neighbor)-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ construction by about 25\%. For state preparation, we consider a Phase gate programmable -H-{CNOT+P}-LC- circuit and derive matching obstructions to attaining the CZ-span counting lower bound of $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ for depth by the entangling gates. For cycle connectivity $C_n$, we prove that the minimum depth is exactly $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil{-}1$ when $n$ is not a multiple of four and $2\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil$ when $n\,{=}\,4k$. We construct a hole-free minimum-perimeter square-lattice patch with a Hamiltonian cycle for every even size, giving optimal-depth programmable circuits to implement Clifford states for all $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$. Exhaustive and heuristic searches address the remaining cases for $n$ up to 256, and selected values up to 1,024 qubits. The improvement against comparable state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth-$(2n{+}2)$ solution, is about 50\%. Finally, combining state synthesis circuits developed in this work with a known four-diagonal-stage decomposition gives rise to a depth $4n{-}4$ for $n\,{=}\,4k{+}2$ and depth $4n$ for $n\,{=}\,4k$ implementation of arbitrary Clifford unitaries. This improves the most relevant state-of-the-art, an LNN-compliant depth $7n{-}4$ construction, by about 43\%.

papers.title: Response-Threshold Framework for First-Peak Preservation in Noisy Grover Search
authors: Nisal De Silva (Faculty of Information Technology
papers.abstract: Grover search is executed only after integer iterations, so noise can alter the stopping decision even when a continuous first peak remains visible. We develop a response-threshold framework separating continuous peak motion, stroboscopic geometry, and the discrete sampled-success argmax. For a Drude-Lorentz environment, linearized HEOM supplies an a priori timing coefficient and sampled-probability differentials. The first-order layer is used as a conservative screen: well-separated points retain the nominal step, whereas near-threshold points escalate to finite-$\lambda$ evaluation. Across 260 unique HEOM points drawn from five overlapping validation sets, it detects all 15 observed stopping changes with zero regret on the changed subset; its residual errors are 45 one-step-early calls on otherwise stable points; the 245-point stable subset has mean regret $4.42\times10^{-3}$. An empirically validated two-stage workflow escalates every observed change while avoiding 160 of 260 unique full-HEOM propagations. Same-bath NZ2 reduces early calls. A heterogeneous three-qubit circuit exhibits three stopping-transition scales, each replicated across eight marked targets, and finite-shot recovery is 96.18% overall, with failures localized to a near-degenerate boundary at $s=1.5$. A depth-refined transfer test supports the predicted local quadratic timing-to-loss relation.

papers.title: Observable Spectral Framework for Noisy Amplitude Amplification: Stopping Stability and Correction
authors: Nisal De Silva (Faculty of Information Technology
Muhammad Aamir Cheema (Faculty of Information Technology
papers.abstract: Stopping rules for noisy amplitude amplification often rely on channel-specific success-probability formulas, limiting their transfer across noise mechanisms. We develop an observable spectral framework for stationary noisy standard amplitude amplification under explicit leading-mode, spectral-separation, and residual-control conditions. Within this class, the first amplification lobe has a damped-oscillatory leading component and a bounded non-leading contribution. We derive how frequency shift, damping, and observable phase offset displace the leading peak, and establish sampled-gap criteria for retaining the ideal integer stopping depth, certifying recalibration, or selecting a robust candidate window. In single-target Grover search, frequency and damping errors have stopping-coordinate sensitivities proportional to the search-space size, whereas phase offsets scale with its square root; residual modes can independently reverse the ordering of neighbouring depths. Analytical constructions, circuit simulations, finite-shot inference, and calibration-derived device-like trajectories examine these predictions and their operational limits. For a 64-element search, an a posteriori sampled-set check selects depth five over six, with success probability increasing from 0.595 to 0.626. The resulting theory links observable spectral dynamics to conditional integer stopping guarantees without requiring a separate microscopic channel solution.

papers.title: Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic
papers.abstract: The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.

papers.title: Vanishing Relative Distance of Uniformly Random CSS LDPC Codes Built from Permutation Matrices
papers.abstract: Classical random regular low-density parity-check codes can have minimum distance growing linearly with block length. We study CSS check matrices formed as full $J\times L$ arrays of arbitrary $P\times P$ permutation matrices, sampled uniformly subject to commutation. For fixed column weight $J\ge3$ and fixed even row weight $L>2J$, we prove that the relative minimum distance converges to zero in probability as $P\to\infty$, with block length $n=LP$. We analyze the weight enumerators that count all nontrivial logical representatives after excluding stabilizers. A coefficientwise lower bound shows that, at every fixed relative weight $0<\alpha<1$ along even-weight sequences, exponentially many such representatives exist with high probability. Their typical and mean counts have exponent lower bound $h_2(\alpha)/2$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We compare this bound with the classical LDPC and dense CSS mean weight-distribution exponents. The existence, with high probability, of a logical operator below every fixed target weight $\delta n$ yields the distance conclusion.

papers.title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
papers.abstract: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $\Omega(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.

papers.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
papers.abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Techniques for Distributed Entanglement Generation and Purification
papers.abstract: We develop a purification-aware optimization framework for distributing high-fidelity entangled states over quantum networks. In repeater-based architectures, the framework jointly selects entanglement swapping, fusion or graph-state growth, and purification operations to maximize generation rate under a fidelity threshold. Different purification models can be incorporated through their fidelity-update, success-probability, and latency rules. We introduce purification-augmented generation trees and dynamic programming (DP) algorithms for entangled-pair (EP) distribution. Hypergraph-flow linear programming (LP) formulations support level-based structures and concurrent generation across multiple trees and demands. We extend the framework to GHZ states and arbitrary graph states constructed from remote EP resources, introduce graph-state construction primitives, and derive closed-form fidelity-vector updates for GHZ fusion and purification and graph-state growth and purification. We provide optimal formulations under the adopted models, discretization, and purification bounds, together with efficient DP and LP heuristics. We bound fidelity- and rate-discretization errors and establish convergence for fixed constructions under stated regularity conditions. NetSquid simulations of EP generation using our LP approach show an average 160% increase in generation rate over the compared prior approaches, with gains up to 330% in some scenarios. GHZ and graph-state simulations demonstrate the heuristics' effectiveness in balancing generation rate, output fidelity, and computational overhead.

papers.title: Graph-Cover-based Characterization of the Bethe Partition Function of Double-Edge Factor Graphs
papers.abstract: For standard factor graphs (S-FGs), whose local functions are nonnegative-real valued, a popular approximation of the partition function is given by the Bethe approximation, which is also known as the Bethe partition function. Vontobel gave a combinatorial characterization of the Bethe partition function with the help of graph covers. The proof of this characterization heavily relied on the method of types. In this paper, we study double-edge factor graphs (DE-FGs), whose local functions are complex valued and satisfy certain positive-semidefinite constraints. DE-FGs and their partition functions are particularly relevant to quantum information processing. Approximating the partition function of a DE-FG is more difficult than approximating the partition function of an S-FG because the DE-FG partition function is a sum of complex values rather than nonnegative-real values. We develop a Bethe approximation of the partition function of a DE-FG based on sum-product-algorithm (SPA) fixed points. However, one cannot directly apply the method of types to prove a similar graph-cover-based combinatorial characterization of the Bethe partition function as in the case of S-FGs. Despite this, we establish such a combinatorial characterization for a class of DE-FGs that satisfy an easily checkable condition. Towards proving this characterization, we apply a suitable loop-calculus transform (LCT) to DE-FGs. Originally, the LCT was introduced by Chertkov and Chernyak as a special linear transform for S-FGs and later extended by Mori. Our proposed LCT is applicable to both S-FGs and DE-FGs and generalizes prior versions by handling zero-valued SPA fixed-point message components, which are common in DE-FGs. Supported by numerical results, we conjecture that the graph-cover-based combinatorial characterization of the Bethe partition function holds more broadly for DE-FGs.

papers.title: Correcting quantum errors one gradient step at a time
papers.abstract: Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) lets a recovery fail with some probability, in exchange for higher fidelity when it succeeds. Prior PAQEC code searches keep the codewords orthonormal with penalty terms and tune the code without its best recovery. We propose a gradient method with three new parts. First, the codewords move on the complex Stiefel manifold, so they are orthonormal at every step without penalties. Second, every code is trained against its best recovery, which we solve for at each step rather than learn. Third, a fast Petz recovery that we can differentiate even for symmetric codes gets the search close, and the exact semidefinite program finishes it. We train a single five-qubit code over generalized amplitude damping noise. At weak noise ($\gamma = 0.1$, $p = 0.05$) and equal success probability, it has $23$ times lower infidelity than the permutation-invariant code of prior work, and $9$ times lower than that work's numerically optimized code. At equal fidelity it succeeds $91\%$ of the time, against $76\%$ for the permutation-invariant code.

papers.title: Elementary Quantum Gates from Lie Group Embeddings in $U(2^n)$: Spectral Geometry and Intrinsic Factorization Lengths
papers.abstract:
We study intrinsic factorizations of quantum gates using determinant-one unitaries supported on arbitrary two-dimensional subspaces of $\C^N$, where $N=2^n$. For $U\in U(N)$ write $r=\operatorname{rank}(U-I)$. When $r\ge2$, we characterize all factors that lower the active rank by two through traceless compressions of the Cayley transform on $\Ran(U-I)$. For the ordered active eigenangles $\vartheta_j\in(0,2\pi)$, existence is equivalent to $\vartheta_1+\vartheta_2\le2\pi\le\vartheta_{r-1}+\vartheta_r$. For $U\in SU(N)$, combining this construction with eigenangle merging realizes the classical reflection-length formula in two-level form: $\ell^{SU}(U)=\max\{
u(U),r-
u(U)\}$, where $
u(U)$ is the positive eigenangle sum divided by $2\pi$. On the full-rank open set, the age indexes $N-1$ connected components with constant intrinsic length. We place these factorizations within the spectral description of the dictionaries formed by faithful $SU(2)$ and $U(2)$ embeddings. For $n\ge2$, these dictionaries are Haar-null of Hausdorff dimensions $N^2-N+1$ and $N^2-N+2$; the former is compact and the latter dense. Distances to compact sectors reduce to eigenvalue matching. Further results concern ambient minimality of embedded geodesics and a first-order sharp spectral bound on coherence production.

papers.title: Multivariate Multicycle Codes for Complete Single-Shot Decoding
papers.abstract: We introduce multivariate multicycle (MM) codes, a Koszul-complex formulation of abelian multicycle (AMC) codes, which are multidimensional scalar lifted-product codes over a finite abelian group algebra, that unifies bivariate bicycle, multivariate bicycle, abelian two-block group algebra, generalized bicycle, trivariate tricycle, and toric codes. MM codes are Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes defined from length-$(t+1)$ chain complexes, and for $t\geq4$ they possess metachecks for both types of checks, which can be used for single-shot decoding. We offer a framework that facilitates the construction of long-length chain complexes through the use of the Koszul complex. In particular, obtaining explicit boundary maps (parity check and metacheck matrices) is particularly straightforward in our approach. We also determine when an MM code encodes logical qubits, count the independent check relations not generated by its metachecks, and show that middle-degree codes with even $t$ have equal $X$ and $Z$ distances. This simple but very general parameterization of codes permitted us to efficiently perform a numerical search, where we identify several MM code candidates with high rates and high code distances. Examples of new codes with parameters $[[n,k,d]]$ include $[[96,12,8]]$, $[[144,12,12]]$, $[[486,24,12]]$, $[[630,70,9]]$, and $[[648,60,9]]$. For selected codes, we report confinement profiles and study single-shot and few-shot decoding under phenomenological and circuit-level noise. Our codes also include explicit collapsed 5D through 9D instances, and our 5D instances have check weights lower than those of recent small instances of quantum Tanner codes.

papers.title: Shot noise can decide capacity comparisons of quantum models
papers.abstract: Shot noise can decide close comparisons of what quantum models appear able to learn. On an IBM processor, the standard estimate of a capacity measure, the effective dimension, placed a 48-qubit model above about 90% of classical networks with as many parameters at 256 shots per circuit. The split-shot estimate from the same data, which removes the bias of the Fisher matrix and needs no noise model, placed it above 12%. A registered run at six parameter points of a 16-qubit model repeated this: the standard estimate placed the three random points above every classical network, the split-shot estimate above 11 to 22%. In simulation the standard estimate reversed the comparison with the classical median at all 100 random points tried. The inflation is the size that shot noise predicts, and a forecast from a pilot run bounds it from above. For squared loss and a linear readout, the error of the standard parameter-shift estimate of a model's Fisher matrix is an exact polynomial in single-shot statistics. Its leading term grows with the effective rank of the matrix, so the shot budget for a stated precision follows from a pilot run; on hardware the observed errors were 0.85 to 1.09 times the predicted ones. The effective dimension can be bracketed from the data but not pinned down at a practical budget. Capacity reports should state their shot count and use the split-shot estimate.

papers.title: Live Noise Fingerprints for Quantum Program Analysis
papers.abstract: Quantum programs are probabilistic in nature, and noisy execution due to current imperfect hardware further complicates their analysis. In this paper, we study abstract semantics for analysing quantum programs under these conditions. We introduce noise fingerprints, compact descriptions of the observable effects of noise relative to a finite interface of input states and output measurements. We use them to define our abstract domain with respect to the concrete noise-related behaviour. We relate the concrete and abstract domains through a probabilistic Galois connection, extending the Galois-connection framework to distribution-valued interpretations. We study the resulting abstraction in terms of observational soundness, conciseness, efficiency, and ability to adapt to changing noise. We show that polynomial-size interfaces yield exponentially smaller fingerprints than full noise models while preserving the chosen observations, and that fingerprint distance characterises the largest observational discrepancy over the chosen interface. Further, we develop ChanShadow, which reuses noise fingerprints of commonly used short program fragments to analyse noisy execution of whole programs and provides a uniform finite-sample error bound. We construct working examples showing how fingerprints support program analysis. We evaluate fingerprint precision, representation cost, measurement requirements, and behaviour under noise drift. On a synthetic benchmark, fingerprints retain $(99 \pm 1)\%$ of the noise strength information of a full noise model. On simulated noise drift, reusing earlier measurements reduces the number of fresh measurement rounds needed to reach an error tolerance of $0.10$ by a factor of $2.3$ at $95\%$ confidence and by a factor of $27$ under the median-error criterion.

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing of Quantum Software based on Stabilizer States
papers.abstract: A major challenge in quantum computing is to systematically check if a quantum program implements its desired functionality. For classical programs, testing is widely used; each test case comprises a pair of sample input and expected output to be compared with the actual output. To increase the number of test cases, however, one has to solve the test-oracle problem: for each additional test input one has to know the correct output. Metamorphic testing tackles this problem by utilizing metamorphic relations between input and output domains to automatically derive new test cases from existing ones. However, adapting metamorphic testing to the quantum realm is not straightforward, since quantum states cannot be directly inspected. We propose a framework of quantum metamorphic testing (QMT) in which the metamorphic relations incorporate the measurement procedures required to assess quantum outputs. We apply our QMT framework to testing the preparation of stabilizer states, which are central to protocols like measurement-based quantum computing or quantum error correction. We utilize structural properties of stabilizer states to systematically derive measurement circuits for new test cases from existing ones. We implement this framework in Qiskit, and demonstrate that it reduces by an order of magnitude the testing run time compared to testing with randomly generated input states. We further show effectiveness by revealing synthetic program faults injected by circuit mutations, as well as a real bug in the Qiskit compiler.

papers.title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a classically controlled gate should become a quantum-controlled gate instead. On all benchmarks, qlin checks that the compiled program computes what its source computes, and the checker is proved sound in Lean 4. At the published per-decision cost of the QICK controller (42 ns), 10 of 65 programs run at least 10% faster than the best baseline in our cost model, up to 91.2%, mostly because one multiway branch replaces a long chain of if statements. On the register-transfer logic of the QubiC controller, a compiled distance-5 repetition decoder selects its correction in 21.3 instead of 151.1 expected cycles. Timing runs on an IBM device were too noisy to confirm or reject the model's ranking.

papers.title: Proxima: Optimizing Syndrome Extraction Circuit Scheduling for Practical Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: The fault-tolerant performance of quantum error correction codes relies critically on the scheduling of parity checks in syndrome extraction circuits (SECs). For general CSS-type quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, the vast scheduling space and intricate error-propagation patterns make it computationally prohibitive to directly optimize the logical error rate (LER) or the exact circuit-level distance ($d_{\mathrm{circ}}$). To address this challenge, we introduce Proxima, a highly effective automated SEC scheduling framework guided by a distance-related metric termed proximity. Defined directly on the detector error model (DEM), proximity quantifies the minimum number of additional faults required to complete a seed fault to an undetectable logical failure, naturally capturing arbitrary circuit-level fault mechanisms and bounding $d_{\mathrm{circ}}$ from above. Proxima synthesizes a pool of valid schedules at a target depth and ranks them by evaluating proximity within small, graph-local DEM fault subsets, progressively enlarging the subset only to break ties among top-ranked candidates. Across a broad spectrum of qLDPC code families, Proxima consistently attains low circuit depths and high circuit-level distance bounds, reducing LER by 1.4--2.6$\times$ over the strongest automated baseline and up to $40\times$ over others while generalizing robustly across noise models and decoders. Furthermore, by exploiting translational symmetry via a compact monomial representation, Proxima discovers depth-8 uniform schedules for bivariate bicycle codes that surpass even IBM's depth-7 reference schedule [Nature, 2024] by 2.1--5.1$\times$, establishing the DEM-level proximity as a practical objective for fault-tolerant compilation.
